note: What this file is: the exact text Malina reads for each page of chapter 1, with delivery cues in square brackets (not spoken) and Mattei written in phonetic symbols so it is said the Italian way. Page 1 reuses the opening already recorded for the sound check.

pages.name: the speech
pages.text: [conversational] You've heard the speech. [wry] Times are tough. Tighten your belts. Cut spending, push up interest rates, hold wages down. Sounds like common sense... [serious] But austerity has a birthday. Economist Clara E. /matˈtɛi/ dug through the archives and found it — right after the First World War. [urgent] And she argues it was never really about budgets. It was about STOPPING something.

pages.name: the war
pages.text: [conversational] Picture Britain in 1915. The war is burning through shells faster than factories can make them. And the government doesn't run out of money. [pause] It runs out of SHELLS. So it takes charge: what factories make, what things cost, what workers are paid. Italy does the same. [thoughtful] And people notice. If the economy can be organised for war... why not for what people need, instead of just for profit?

pages.name: Britain after the war
pages.text: [urgent] When the war ends, workers don't want to go back. In Britain, union membership doubles, to eight million. In Glasgow, sixty thousand people pack a square, demanding a shorter working week. The government sends in troops. [pause] And tanks. Coal miners demand public ownership of the mines. A royal commission backs them. [wry] The government ignores it.

pages.name: Italy
pages.text: [serious] In Italy, it goes further. In 1919, more than a million workers go on strike. In 1920, half a million take over their factories.

pages.name: the capital order
pages.text: [conversational] Now look at it from the owners' side. This isn't just about pay. It threatens what /matˈtɛi/ calls the capital order: a few people own the land, the factories and the mines... and everyone else must work for a wage to survive. [urgent] If workers can run things themselves, that order could fall.

pages.name: the experts
pages.text: [conversational] So the experts get together. Brussels, 1920: thirty-nine countries send delegates, mostly bankers and treasury officials. [wry] Guess who isn't in the room? Not one trade unionist. [conversational] Genoa, 1922: same advice. And it's simple. Balance the budget. Cut public spending. Stop creating new money. Hand interest rates to central banks, out of reach of voters. And get back on gold.

pages.name: three parts
pages.text: [conversational] /matˈtɛi/ says the plan has three parts. Spending: cut public services, and tax everyday purchases instead of wealth. Money: make borrowing expensive, so businesses slow down and jobs disappear. Work: cut wages, sell off what the public owns, weaken the unions.

pages.name: the official story
pages.text: [conversational] The official story sounds reasonable. Prices are rising, war debts are huge, and a government, like a household, has to balance its books. Right? [serious] But economists who study how modern money works say a country that issues its own money isn't a household. It can't run out of its own money. It can run out of workers, materials and machines, as the war just showed. [wry] And gold? Gold was a limit they CHOSE. Going back to it meant forcing wages and prices down.

pages.name: why
pages.text: [serious] So why do it? Ask /matˈtɛi/, and her answer is blunt: power. Take away the alternatives, like public housing and help for the unemployed, and people must take whatever job is going, at whatever wage. [wry] The message to workers: work more, consume less.

pages.name: sound familiar
pages.text: [serious] That's the argument /matˈtɛi/ makes. Austerity was never really about the books. It was about power. [pause] Sound familiar? [curious] But wait. If a country can't run out of its own money... won't creating it just cause inflation? [conversational] That's next.
